subject: is there any difference between these ways to specify priors

messages.author: 43f5744093db5550
messages.subject: is there any difference between these ways to specify priors
parts:
beta0 below are regression coefficients. Does the difference among different prior specification have any impact on mixing or convergence?

#method 1

parameters {

    vector [100] beta0;

}

   

model {

beta0 ~ normal(0,32);

...

}

 # method 2

parameters {

    vector [100] beta0;

}

 

model {

for ( i in 1:100) beta0[i]~ normal(0,32);

...

}

 #method 3 

parameters {

    vector [100] beta0;

}

 

transformed data {

            cov_matrix [100] sigma0;

            vector [100] z0;

            z0 <- rep_vector(0.0, 100);

            sigma0 <- diag_matrix( rep_vector(32^2, 100) );

}

 

model {

beta0 ~ multi_normal(z0,sigma0);

...

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is there any difference between these ways to specify priors
parts:
There is a section (section 19.2 in the manual for Stan v2.0.1) discussing vectorization
in the "Optimizing Stan Code" chapter of the manual. There is a discussion of
arrays vs. vectors in the chapter on containers (chapter 8 in v2.0.1).

One note about your #method 3: Given that the mean is fixed at 0,
you'd want to declare that as a transformed data parameter rather than
a local variable. Transformed data is not auto-diffed, so is much
more efficient than using a local variable, which will be an auto-diff
variable if declared in the model block. See figure 24.3 in v2.0.1.

Sorry the doc's so long!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: is there any difference between these ways to specify priors
parts:
thanks. I guess I could be more specific. Let me summarize what I read to make sure I understand correctly.

when 1) we have a set of parameters that we expect their posterior samples to be highly correlated, 2) we use non-informative prior on each of them separately (they do not share info via hyper parameters), whether we start with many univariate priors or one single multivariate prior will give us the same effective sample size from the same number of iterations ( I understand vectorization affects the time to run the same number of iterations). And will this change if we run hierarchical models with hyper parameters? 

I ask this because some other optimization algorithms seem to recommend grouping them into one single multivariate node.
thanks
wei

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: is there any difference between these ways to specify priors
parts:
The model and the way its coded are two issues. You get the
same number of effective samples per iteration with vectorized
vs. unvectorized code, because you'll get exactly the same samples.
Stan's behavior is fully determined by the log probability function
and the random number generation seed.

The vectorized code will take less time per iteration.

The model dictates how the statements have to be grouped,
then just vectorize as much as you can given the model for
efficiency.

Reparameterization in hierarchical regressions is also often
very useful --- see the chapter in the manual.

- Bob
